citations.verbatim_quote: [Jack Black, You Can't Win (1926), p. 172:] In speaking of the cook ovens I may say that it was there the word "yegg" originated. It has not yet been locked in the dictionary, but it has a place in our language and it's about time its derivation was settled once and for all. It is a corruption of "yekk," a word from one of the many dialects spoken in Chinatown, and it means beggar. When a hypo or beggar approached a Chinaman to ask for something to eat, he was greeted with the exclamation, "yekk man, yekk man." [Contrast Stedman & Lee, Canton Dialect Phrase Book (New York, 1888), pp. 66–67:] 11. A thief broke in my shop and stole all I had. / 十二 有賊入舖將我的嘢一概偷哂 ('yau ch'ák yap p'u'...).
citations.linguistic_note: Falsifies the popular San Francisco Chinatown 'yekk = beggar' origin story popularized by ex-safecracker Jack Black in You Can't Win (1926): (1) chronologically published 26 years after the 1900 baseline (and 33 years after New England rail-tramp 'yeager' in the Jan. 23, 1893 Hartford Courant and 32 years after 'yegg' in the Jan. 14, 1894 Cincinnati Enquirer); (2) Black falsely asserts in 1926 that yegg 'has not yet been locked in the dictionary' (it had been in Century Supplement 1909 and Webster's New International 1909 for 17 years); (3) lexically, no Cantonese or Siyi dialect word yekk/yik/yak means 'beggar' or 'thief'—at Chinatown cook-ovens, yak fán! (喫飯, Williams 1856 p. 674) means 'eat rice / take food!', which Black retroactively folk-etymologized onto preexisting hobo yeggman.
citations.analysis_notes: FALSIFIED-MYTH PRIMARY SOURCE TRACE (Donor-Lexicon Audit): Traces the famous Chinatown 'yekk man = beggar' anecdote directly to Jack Black's 1926 memoir You Can't Win (youcantwin0000jack, leaf n5–n6 Macmillan 1926 title/imprint; leaf n189 p. 172), quoted in Green's Dictionary of Slang, Grammarphobia, and Slang City. Fails both deterministic gates: chronologically implausible (1926 > 1900; pre-1900 Eastern/Midwestern rail-tramp attestations in CT 1893 and OH 1894 predate Black's memoir by over three decades) and unattested in historical Cantonese lexicons (Stedman & Lee's 1888 New York Chinatown phrasebook, leaves n4, n101–n102, confirms U.S. Cantonese speakers used 賊 ch'ák/ts'ák for 'thief', while cook-shop yak fán means 'eat rice!').
